title: Shloka 40
subtitle: Lightning above the six wheels, and the name at last

namas.gloss: Radiant As A Streak Of Lightning
namas.translation: Her brilliance is the brilliance of lightning drawn out like a vine, thin and sudden and impossible to look away from.

compound.gloss: she whose radiance equals a creeper of lightning

children.gloss: equal to a creeper of lightning
equal to, on a level with

namas.translation: She rests beyond the six wheels strung along the spine, higher than the whole ladder she has just climbed.

compound.gloss: firmly placed above the six wheels

children.gloss: a wheel, a mystic circle in the body

namas.translation: Her hold on her own is a great one, an attachment that does not slacken however far she rises.

morphology.note: The Devanagari admits two resolutions, mahā + āsakti and mahā + sakti, both meaning a great clinging; many editions instead read mahāśaktiḥ, 'the great power', which fits the surrounding kuṇḍalinī names.

namas.translation: She lies wound like a sleeping snake at the base of the spine until the moment she straightens and climbs.

morphology.note: A possessive derivative of kuṇḍala, 'a ring or coil', built with the suffix -in and its feminine -ī; not a compound.

namas.translation: She is subtler than the thread that trails from a broken lotus stalk, too fine for the eye to follow.

morphology.note: tanīyas is the comparative of tanu, 'slender', and takes its first member in an ablative sense.

compound.gloss: finer than the fibre of a lotus stalk

children.gloss: the fibre of a lotus stalk
the stalk or shoot of a lotus

commentary.meaning: Two verses have described an ascent without once naming the thing that ascends. This verse supplies the name, but not before three others. She is first given an appearance: her brightness is that of lightning drawn out like a climbing vine, thin and vertical and gone before the eye adjusts. Then a position, above the six wheels — which settles the question the previous verse left open, since it counts six and puts her past them rather than making the crown a seventh. Then a disputed name whose likeliest sense is a great clinging, an attachment that survives the undoing of every knot. Only then, in the middle of the second line and in four syllables, comes kuṇḍalinī, the coiled one, the word the whole passage has been circling. And the verse does not end there either. It ends by calling her finer than the thread inside a lotus stalk, so that the lightning of the opening and the near-invisible fibre of the close frame everything between them. Blinding and imperceptible, in the space of thirty-two syllables.
commentary.history:
Taḍit is lightning and latā is a creeper, the climbing vine that winds up a tree; the compound sets them in apposition, lightning that is a vine, and the point of comparison is shape as much as brilliance. A lightning stroke is thin, vertical and branching, and so is the ascending power the previous verses described. The image is not this hymn's invention. It is the standard figure for kuṇḍalinī across the literature, and the Saundaryalaharī uses the same word in the same context, calling her a slender streak of lightning stationed above the six lotuses. Readers comparing editions will find the first syllable spelled either taḍit or taṭit, with retroflex ḍ or retroflex ṭ; both are attested, the variation is old, and nothing turns on it.

Ṣaṭcakroparisaṃsthitā is the hymn's own statement of how the centres are counted. Six wheels, and she is above them — not the seventh in a series but past the series altogether. This is the ordinary reckoning in the tradition, and it explains a small puzzle in modern popular accounts, which usually list seven cakras and thereby flatten a distinction the sources cared about. The six are enumerable, each with its element, its petal count and its syllable; what is above them is not another item of the same kind. The verb in saṃsthitā carries the prefix sam, which intensifies: not merely placed but settled, established, standing firm.

The third name is the one where editions part company. The text as printed here reads mahāsaktiḥ with a dental s, and admits two resolutions — mahā plus āsakti, or mahā plus sakti, both from √sañj, to cling or adhere — either of which gives a great attachment. A great many editions and reciters instead have mahāśaktiḥ with a palatal ś, the great power, which slides comfortably into the surrounding vocabulary and is what most people assume they are singing. The difference is one letter and it changes the name entirely. Where the reading with the dental is kept, it is generally explained as her attachment to Śiva, and read that way it is a pointed thing to place here: eleven names have described the untying of every knot that binds, and the twelfth affirms one bond that is not untied. The tradition's technical term for what the yogin must abandon is turned into a name of the goddess. It is worth saying plainly that this is a real textual disagreement rather than a matter of interpretation, and that a reader will hear both readings from teachers of equal standing.

Kuṇḍalinī is not a compound. It is kuṇḍala, a ring or a coil or the coiled ornament worn in the ear, with the possessive suffix -in and its feminine -ī: the one who has a coil, the coiled one. The picture behind the word is a snake asleep at the base of the spine, wound three and a half times around, with its mouth stopping the opening of the central channel — so that the same body that blocks the road is the traveller who will take it. Eleven names of ascent have gone by before the word is spoken, and when it comes it is the shortest name in the passage, four syllables in the middle of a line, given no emphasis at all.

Bisa is the stalk of the lotus, and if you break one the pith draws out into filaments that hang between the halves before they snap. Sanskrit poets used those threads as the standard measure of something at the edge of perception but still continuous, still one thing. Tanīyasī is the comparative of tanu, slender, so the name says finer than that. The claim is about subtlety rather than smallness — the same order of statement as the Śvetāśvatara's description of the individual soul as a fraction of a fraction of the tip of a hair, which nonetheless has infinity in it. And the placement matters: the verse that began with lightning ends by saying she is too fine to see. Neither image cancels the other, and the passage as a whole seems designed to prevent the reciter from settling into either.
commentary.practice:
The pattern of the two preceding verses breaks here. There, four names filled four quarters exactly; here five names occupy the same thirty-two syllables, and the second line divides four, four, eight — mahāsaktiḥ, kuṇḍalinī, bisatantutanīyasī. Reciters carrying momentum from the long names of the ascent tend to crowd the two short ones together into something that sounds like a single word. Give each of the four-syllable names its own space. The name of the whole subject of the passage is one of them.

Two names in this verse end in visarga: taḍillatāsamaruciḥ and mahāsaktiḥ. Visarga is not silence and not an English h. It is a voiceless breath that echoes the vowel before it, so ruciḥ closes with a faint unvoiced i after the h, something like ru-chih(i), and saktiḥ likewise. Dropping it is the single most common fault in recitation of this hymn, and it matters more here than usual because in both cases the visarga is the grammatical marker that identifies these as nominatives of i-stems rather than the ā-stems that surround them.

Ṣaṭcakropari opens with a cluster that gives trouble in every language: the retroflex ṭ immediately followed by the palatal c. The tongue-tip is curled back for the first and must land at the hard palate for the second with no vowel between. The underlying numeral is ṣaṣ, six, whose final consonant becomes ṭ before the c of cakra; knowing that keeps you from inserting the vowel your mouth wants. Then kro carries a long o, which in Sanskrit is always long, and pari ends the compound before saṃ begins — the anusvāra there is a nasal made in the position of the following sth, so it is closer to n than to m.

Kuṇḍalinī has ṇḍ, two retroflexes in succession, and the temptation is to make the first one dental because English has no other kind of n before d. Curl the tongue back once and hold it for both. Taḍillatā gives you a genuine doubled l, produced by the sandhi of taḍit and latā, and a doubled consonant in Sanskrit is held twice as long: ta-ḍil-la-tā, with the l audibly sustained across the syllable break.

This verse is unusually instructive for the archanā forms, because its five names decline in four different ways. The ā-stem takes -āyai: ṣaṭcakroparisaṃsthitāyai namaḥ. The two i-stems take -yai on a stem whose final i becomes a glide: taṭillatāsamarucyai namaḥ, mahāsaktyai namaḥ. The two ī-stems take -yai likewise but with the long vowel shortening to the glide: kuṇḍalinyai namaḥ, bisatantutanīyasyai namaḥ. Working through all five once slowly does more for the feminine dative than memorising a paradigm.

As for what the verse asks: it offers two pictures of her and refuses to reconcile them, and it gives no instruction whatever. Nobody is told to raise anything, look for lightning, or expect a coil to stir. The names are descriptions in the third person of what is the case, and a reciter who treats them as a report of what should be happening in his own spine has mistaken the grammar. The one thing the verse does ask, by its metre, is that the name kuṇḍalinī not be hurried.

crossReferences.iast: taṭillekhātanvīṃ tapanaśaśivaiśvānaramayīṃ niṣaṇṇāṃ ṣaṇṇāmapyupari kamalānāṃ tava kalām | mahāpadmāṭavyāṃ mṛditamalamāyena manasā mahāntaḥ paśyanto dadhati paramāhlādalaharīm ||
crossReferences.translation: Your portion, slender as a streak of lightning, made of sun and moon and fire, seated above the six lotuses in the forest of great lotuses — the great ones, beholding it with a mind whose stain and illusion have been ground away, hold within them a wave of the highest delight.
crossReferences.relevance: As close to a direct parallel as the two texts come. The verse has taṭillekhā, a streak of lightning, and ṣaṇṇām apy upari kamalānām, above the six lotuses, in that order — the first two names of this shloka, in the same sequence, in a different metre. It also supplies what the sahasranāma withholds: a statement of who sees this and what seeing it does to them.

crossReferences.deva: बालाग्रशतभागस्य शतधा कल्पितस्य च । भागो जीवः स विज्ञेयः स चानन्त्याय कल्पते ॥
crossReferences.iast: bālāgraśatabhāgasya śatadhā kalpitasya ca | bhāgo jīvaḥ sa vijñeyaḥ sa cānantyāya kalpate ||
crossReferences.translation: Take the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, and divide that a hundred ways: the living self is to be known as one such part — and that part is fit for infinity.
crossReferences.relevance: The idiom behind bisatantutanīyasī, and the reason the name is a claim about subtlety rather than about size. The Upaniṣad's arithmetic of diminishing fractions exists to make a point about what is not measured by them; the second half of the verse turns round and says this vanishing quantity is capable of the endless. The hymn compresses the same movement into one comparative adjective.

references.title: Roots of Yoga
references.author: tr. and ed. James Mallinson and Mark Singleton (Penguin Classics, 2017)
references.note: A sourcebook of translated passages arranged by topic, with substantial chapters on the subtle body and on kuṇḍalinī drawn from dozens of texts across a thousand years. The most efficient way to see how much the descriptions vary — how many coils, which channel, what wakes her — and therefore the best corrective to the impression that this verse is quoting a settled doctrine.

references.title: Saundaryalaharī (Devanagari with Roman transliteration)
references.author: Śṛṅgeri Śāradā Pīṭham
references.note: Verse 21 is quoted above; read it together with verses 9 and 10, which cover the ascent and the descent of nectar. Between them the three verses restate the whole of shlokas 38 to 40 of the sahasranāma in a more demanding metre and with a poet's willingness to say what the litany only implies.

references.title: Lalitā Sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's Commentary (Saubhāgyabhāskara)
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library / Theosophical Publishing House)
references.note: The usual English access to the eighteenth-century commentary that later expositions lean on. Consult it when you hit a name like the third here, where the manuscripts disagree: what you get is not a critical apparatus but a display of how many defensible derivations a single name will bear, which is itself worth understanding about this literature.

references.title: The Hindu Tantric World: An Overview
references.author: André Padoux (University of Chicago Press, 2017)
references.note: Padoux's late, short synthesis, written after a career on this material. His chapter on the tantric body is the soberest available account of what the six centres were for, and he is explicit that they are ritual and meditative constructions rather than a discovered physiology — the assumption this verse requires and never states.

references.title: A Sanskrit–English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Look up bisa and kuṇḍala. The first shows that the word means the lotus stalk itself, not only its fibre, which sharpens the image; the second shows that kuṇḍala is an everyday object, a ring or an earring, so that kuṇḍalinī is a plain descriptive nickname rather than a technical coinage.
